Scroll-linked shaders with no scroll listener

Scroll the page. Each block below is HTML drawn through a fragment shader, and the shader's inputs are CSS custom properties that scroll-driven animations, a scroll-state() container query and a scroll-triggered animation set. The page has no scroll listener and no observer. Scroll fast to blur the blocks by the scroll speed. The buttons and fields keep working.

Scroll this page

This block melts as it leaves the top of the screen. A view timeline moves --fx-progress over the exit range.

Sticky bar

Burn in

A view timeline moves --fx-progress from 0 to 1 as this block comes up from the bottom edge. Scroll back down and it burns away again.

Mosaic

The same timeline and the same property. The shader samples the block in square cells that shrink from 40 px to 1 px.

Rows

Rows 14 px tall start off to the left and to the right and slide home. Stop half way and press the button: it's where the layout says, the shader only moves pixels.

Unroll

The block is a sheet rolled up at its top edge. The cylinder rolls down the page as you scroll and winds back up when you scroll the other way.

The grey band is the back of the sheet. Its shading is the cylinder's.

Triggered, not scrubbed

This one runs for 900 ms by the clock. A timeline trigger starts it when the whole block is on screen and resets it when the block has left.

Show the code CSS timelines → custom properties → shader
  1. The markup. Ordinary sections. fx names the shader, the classes name the CSS that drives it.
  2. A view timeline sets --fx-progress. The fx library registers the property as a number and passes it to the shader as u_progress.
  3. The page's scroll position as a property.
  4. Scroll speed from a transition. A second property follows the first one 120 ms late. Their difference is the speed.
  5. A scroll-state() query sets --fx-amount on the sticky bar.
  6. A timeline trigger starts a timed animation.
  7. A shader that reads the progress. GLSL for WebGL and WGSL for WebGPU.
  8. The blur that reads the speed.
  9. The roll.
  10. The sticky bar's shader.
  11. The page script. It picks the drawing route and loads the library. Nothing in it reads the scroll position.
  12. Inside the library: the upload and the draw.

How it works

  • Each block with an fx attribute is moved into a canvas by the fx library. The canvas takes the block's place in the page, so it scrolls with the page on the compositor like any other box.
  • The library reads four registered custom properties from the block once per frame while it is on screen and redraws when one changed. It doesn't know where the values come from. Here they come from animation-timeline: view(), animation-timeline: scroll(), a scroll-state(stuck: top) query and animation-trigger.
  • The percentage in each block's corner is the same property printed by a CSS counter inside the block. It changes the block's picture, so the block is uploaded to the texture again on those frames.
  • The shaders only move pixels. The blocks stay where layout put them for hit testing, so a button that is half burnt away is pressed at its normal position.

Live checks

Each check builds a small scroller of its own in a corner of the window and scrolls that. The page isn't scrolled.

ResultExperimentDetail

Findings

From Chromium 157 with software rendering. The rows above say what your browser does.

  • Works: a view timeline on an element that is a canvas child. The element has no box on the page outside its canvas, and its view timeline still follows the scroll position of the page.
  • Works: scroll speed from two custom properties. A property with a transition that is set to var() of a scroll-animated property follows it late. The transition has to be on a descendant of the element that carries the animation.
  • Works: scroll-state(stuck) across the canvas. The query container is the sticky holder outside the canvas. The bar it styles is inside the canvas.
  • Works: timeline-trigger with animation-trigger. The animation runs by the clock and the shader follows it. Where the properties are missing the block falls back to the scrubbed timeline.
  • Not available: the overscroll area. The plan for this page included a drawer on the overscroll area that stretches with the pull. No overscroll-area property exists in Chromium 157, so it wasn't built.
  • Not verified here: whether the effects keep up with a touch scroll on a phone. The scroll moves on the compositor thread and the custom properties are read on the main thread, so the shader may be a frame or more behind the block's position. The WebGPU route on screen is also unverified in the test browser.
